title: Lesson 6: Supporting New and Less-Experienced Staff
summary: Everyone was once new. Help colleagues learn with patience, demonstration and constructive feedback — without mockery, exclusion, or doing their work for them.

items.label: Duration
items.body: 45–60 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Focus
items.body: Teamwork, patience, mentoring, knowledge-sharing, inclusion, professional respect and staff development

sections.title: 1. Introduction: Everyone was once new
paragraphs: Imagine a new therapist who has just joined Zura Spa.
She has completed her initial training, but she is still learning the spa's daily routines.
On her first busy day, she struggles to remember the correct procedure for preparing a treatment room between appointments.
She approaches an experienced colleague and asks: "Please, can you remind me of the correct order for preparing the room?"
The experienced therapist responds: "How many times will they teach you? Didn't you learn anything during training? This is something everybody should know."
The new therapist becomes embarrassed.
Other employees overhear the conversation.
She apologises and walks away.
Later, she encounters another difficulty but decides not to ask anyone because she is afraid of being mocked again.
She makes a mistake that could have been prevented if she had received proper guidance.
Now consider a different response.

The experienced therapist says: "Of course. Let me show you the procedure again. First, check the cleaning requirements, then prepare the fresh linen and supplies according to our checklist. I'll watch you do it this time so you can become more confident."
The new therapist follows the instructions.
She asks a question about a step she does not understand.
Her colleague explains patiently.
Afterward, the experienced therapist says: "You're improving. Keep using the checklist, and ask whenever something is unclear."
The new therapist becomes more confident.
She learns the procedure correctly and is better prepared for her next assignment.
Both situations involved the same new employee and the same question.
The difference was the attitude of the experienced colleague.
An experienced employee can either make a new colleague feel supported enough to learn or afraid enough to hide what she does not understand.
At Zura Spa, every employee has a role in creating a workplace where new and less-experienced colleagues can learn, improve and become dependable members of the team.

sections.title: 2. Who is a new or less-experienced employee?
paragraphs: A new employee is someone who has recently joined the organisation and is still becoming familiar with its people, procedures, expectations and working environment.
A less-experienced employee is someone who may have limited practical experience with a particular responsibility.
These are not always the same.
A therapist may have worked in another spa for three years but recently joined Zura Spa.
She may be experienced in massage therapy but unfamiliar with Zura Spa's booking procedures, service standards and room-preparation requirements.
Another employee may have worked at Zura Spa for several months but still need additional guidance with a particular responsibility.
Being new does not mean being incapable, and being experienced does not mean knowing everything.
Every employee has areas in which she can learn and improve.

sections.title: 3. What does supporting new staff mean?
paragraphs: Supporting new staff means helping them understand their responsibilities, learn workplace procedures, develop confidence and become capable of performing their duties correctly.
Supporting new staff is not simply being friendly.
It involves practical actions that help them become effective employees.
The goal is to help a colleague develop competence, confidence and accountability.
list: Welcoming new employees respectfully.
Explaining workplace expectations.
Demonstrating approved procedures.
Answering reasonable questions.
Providing constructive feedback.
Correcting mistakes respectfully.
Encouraging independent learning.
Helping new employees understand whom to contact for assistance.
Including them in appropriate team activities.
Reporting training needs to supervisors.

sections.title: 4. Why supporting new staff matters at Zura Spa
list: It improves learning. New employees understand procedures more quickly when guidance is clear and practical.
It protects service standards. Proper training reduces preventable mistakes that may affect clients.
It builds trust. New employees become more comfortable asking appropriate questions and reporting difficulties.
It strengthens teamwork. Employees learn to cooperate rather than compete unnecessarily.
It increases team capability. As new employees become competent, they can handle responsibilities more independently.
It creates a healthier workplace. Employees feel more respected when learning is encouraged rather than ridiculed.

sections.title: 5. Remember how you felt when you were new
paragraphs: Before becoming experienced, every employee had to learn.
Think about your first day at a workplace.
If you were joining Zura Spa today, how would you want your colleagues to treat you?
Would you want them to ignore you, mock your questions or deliberately withhold information?
Or would you prefer patience, respect and clear instructions?
Treat new colleagues with the same professionalism you would appreciate when learning something unfamiliar.
An experienced employee should remember that familiarity comes with time, practice and guidance.
list: Will I understand the procedures?
Will my colleagues accept me?
What happens if I make a mistake?
Who can I ask for help?
Will I be embarrassed if I ask a question?
How long will it take before I feel confident?

sections.title: 6. The difference between helping someone learn and doing their work
paragraphs: There is an important distinction between support and dependence.
A new receptionist is learning how to record appointments.
An experienced receptionist can demonstrate the procedure and guide her through several practice bookings.
However, if the experienced employee permanently takes over every booking because the new employee is slower, the new employee may not develop the required competence.
Effective support helps people become capable of doing their work, not permanently dependent on others to do it.
table: Takes over the entire task unnecessarily
Keeps the employee reliant on others

sections.title: 7. Welcoming new employees properly
paragraphs: The way a new employee is received can influence her confidence and willingness to participate.

Poor welcome: A new therapist arrives for her first shift. Colleagues ignore her. Nobody explains where essential supplies are kept. When she asks a question, someone responds: "You'll figure it out."
Professional welcome: A colleague introduces herself, explains relevant routines and helps the new therapist understand where to obtain information.
She may say: "Welcome to Zura Spa. I'll show you the room-preparation area and introduce you to the supervisor. If you're unsure about a procedure, please ask before proceeding."
A welcoming workplace does not mean lowering standards. It means helping employees understand how to meet them.
list: Greet the person respectfully.
Introduce relevant team members.
Explain where to find approved procedures.
Clarify reporting relationships.
Avoid overwhelming the employee with unnecessary information.
Encourage appropriate questions.
Include the employee in relevant team communication.

sections.title: 8. Patience is essential when teaching
paragraphs: People learn at different speeds.
One employee may understand a procedure after one demonstration.
Another may need additional explanation and practice.
This does not automatically mean the second employee is lazy or incapable.
A new therapist struggles to remember the approved room-reset procedure.
An impatient colleague says: "I've explained this already. What's wrong with you?"
A patient colleague says: "Let's go through the checklist again. Show me which step is confusing, and we'll practise it."
Patience does not mean ignoring repeated mistakes indefinitely.
It means giving reasonable guidance, checking understanding and escalating ongoing training needs appropriately.
Correcting someone patiently is more productive than humiliating them for not learning immediately.

sections.title: 9. Avoid mocking or embarrassing less-experienced staff
paragraphs: Mockery can discourage employees from asking questions and reporting mistakes.
These statements attack the person rather than explaining the required standard.
A correction should help someone improve, not make the person feel worthless.

items.label: Inappropriate
items.body: "Even a child should know this." / "You're too slow." / "How did you even get this job?" / "You don't know anything." / "We didn't struggle like this when we started." / "You're always confused."

items.label: Better alternatives
items.body: "Let me explain that step again." / "This part needs correction. Here's the correct procedure." / "Which part are you finding difficult?" / "Let's practise it together." / "You need to improve your speed, but accuracy comes first. Let's work on both." / "Please check the procedure before your next attempt."

sections.title: 10. Teaching by demonstration
paragraphs: Some workplace tasks are easier to understand when demonstrated: preparing a treatment room, arranging supplies, following a cleaning checklist, recording appointments, completing shift handovers, and using authorised workplace systems.
An experienced receptionist teaches a new colleague how to record an appointment.
She explains the required details, demonstrates the booking process and then allows the new employee to complete a supervised practice entry.
She checks the result and corrects any mistakes.
This approach develops understanding rather than encouraging memorisation without practice.

items.label: 1. Explain
items.body: Describe what the employee needs to do and why it matters.

items.label: 2. Demonstrate
items.body: Show the correct approved procedure.

items.label: 3. Let them practise
items.body: Allow the employee to perform the task with appropriate supervision.

items.label: 4. Give feedback
items.body: Identify what was done correctly and what needs improvement.

items.label: 5. Confirm understanding
items.body: Ask the employee to explain or demonstrate the procedure again.

sections.title: 11. Encouraging questions instead of assumptions
paragraphs: New employees may hesitate to ask questions because they do not want to appear inexperienced.
However, guessing can create unnecessary mistakes.
A new therapist is unsure whether a particular treatment-room setup is appropriate for a booked service.
Instead of assuming, she asks the designated trainer or supervisor.
This is responsible behaviour.
It is better for an employee to ask a reasonable question than to proceed with an unsafe or incorrect assumption.
list: Listen to the question.
Avoid unnecessary sarcasm.
Explain the relevant procedure.
Refer to approved instructions when available.
Encourage the employee to confirm understanding.
Escalate questions beyond your authority.

sections.title: 12. Sharing knowledge without feeling threatened
paragraphs: Some experienced employees may become uncomfortable when new colleagues learn quickly.
They may fear losing recognition, influence or opportunities.
This can lead to unhealthy competition.
An experienced receptionist knows an efficient way to organise appointment confirmations.
A new receptionist asks for guidance.
The experienced employee refuses to explain because she wants to remain the only person who knows the procedure.
This weakens the team.
Better approach: she shares the approved method and helps the new employee understand it.
Another employee becoming competent does not reduce the value of your own competence.
A strong team benefits when knowledge is shared appropriately.

sections.title: 13. Avoid creating cliques that exclude new employees
paragraphs: A clique is a small group that behaves in a way that may exclude others.
Existing employees may naturally develop friendships.
However, those friendships should not become a reason to isolate new colleagues.
Several employees regularly discuss important work updates privately.
A new therapist is excluded.
She misses information about a change in the room-preparation procedure.
Later, she is criticised for following the old process.
This is unfair.
Workplace belonging should not depend on being part of a particular friendship group.
list: Share operational information through approved channels.
Include employees who need the information.
Avoid deliberately excluding colleagues.
Do not use inside jokes to embarrass new employees.
Treat everyone professionally regardless of personal friendships.

sections.title: 14. Correcting mistakes without destroying confidence
paragraphs: New employees will sometimes make mistakes while learning.
Correction is necessary, but the manner of correction matters.
Poor correction: "You've done everything wrong. I don't know why they employed you."

Constructive correction: "The appointment details are incomplete. You recorded the service and time correctly, but the required confirmation information is missing. Let me show you where to enter it."
The second response identifies the specific problem and explains how to correct it.
A serious safety or confidentiality mistake may require immediate intervention and formal reporting.
Respectful correction does not mean delaying necessary protective action.
list: Specific.
Respectful.
Factual.
Relevant to the task.
Clear about the expected standard.
Focused on improvement.

sections.title: 15. Avoid comparing new employees unfairly
paragraphs: Employees develop at different rates.
A supervisor tells a new receptionist: "Your colleague learned this in two days. Why are you still struggling after a week?"
This comparison may create embarrassment without identifying what the employee actually needs.
Better approach: "You've improved in recording appointment details, but confirmation accuracy still needs work. Let's review that part of the process and set a clear improvement goal."
Measure progress against the required standard, not against another employee's personality or learning speed.
Comparisons may occasionally help identify training needs, but they should not be used to humiliate people.

sections.title: 16. Supporting new staff without neglecting your own responsibilities
paragraphs: Experienced employees must balance mentoring with their assigned duties.
A therapist has a client arriving in fifteen minutes.
A new colleague asks for help with a non-urgent supply arrangement.
The experienced therapist can say: "I have an appointment to prepare for. Let me finish that first. I'll help you afterward, or you can ask the supervisor if you need assistance sooner."
This is appropriate teamwork.
Supporting new colleagues should not require abandoning essential responsibilities or compromising client care.
When training demands more time than colleagues can reasonably provide, supervisors should arrange structured support.

sections.title: 17. Recognising the limits of your knowledge and authority
paragraphs: An experienced employee should not teach procedures she does not fully understand or is not authorised to perform.
A new therapist asks an experienced colleague about an unfamiliar massage technique.
The colleague has not received approved training in that technique.
She should not improvise an explanation or encourage the new employee to practise on a client.
Instead, she should refer the question to the appropriate qualified trainer or supervisor.
Being experienced does not mean having authority to train others in every area.
list: Client consent and professional boundaries.
Health-related concerns.
Payment adjustments.
Confidential client records.
Equipment safety.
Unfamiliar treatment procedures.
Workplace emergencies.

sections.title: 18. The GUIDE method
paragraphs: A new receptionist is learning appointment confirmations.

An experienced colleague greets her, understands which part of the confirmation process is unclear, instructs by demonstrating the approved procedure, develops independence through supervised confirmations, and encourages by reviewing results, recognising correct work and identifying areas for improvement.
This is effective workplace mentoring.

items.label: G — Greet and include
items.body: Welcome the employee and help her feel respected as a member of the team.

items.label: U — Understand the learning need
items.body: Identify what the employee already knows and where guidance is needed.

items.label: I — Instruct and demonstrate
items.body: Explain the approved procedure clearly and show how it is performed.

items.label: D — Develop independence
items.body: Allow supervised practice and gradually increase responsibility as competence improves.

items.label: E — Encourage and evaluate
items.body: Provide constructive feedback, recognise progress and identify remaining training needs.

sections.title: 19. Responsibilities of new employees
paragraphs: Supporting new staff is not only the responsibility of experienced colleagues.
New employees must also demonstrate willingness to learn.
A new therapist receives an explanation of the room-preparation checklist.
She should make an effort to understand the steps and use the checklist.
If she repeatedly forgets a step, she should identify what is confusing and seek appropriate guidance.
Experienced employees should be willing to teach, and new employees should be willing to learn.
Both responsibilities are necessary.
list: Listen attentively during training.
Ask questions when unsure.
Follow approved procedures.
Take reasonable notes.
Practise assigned tasks.
Accept corrections respectfully.
Avoid pretending to understand what remains unclear.
Report mistakes promptly.
Respect colleagues' time.
Demonstrate improvement through consistent effort.

sections.title: 20. When additional training or supervisory intervention is necessary
paragraphs: Not every learning difficulty can be resolved through informal assistance.
A new therapist continues to struggle with a required procedure after several demonstrations.
Instead of repeatedly criticising her, the supervisor should assess whether additional structured training, clearer instructions or supervised practice is needed.
Support does not mean allowing an employee to perform work independently before she has demonstrated the required competence.
Client safety and service standards must remain protected.
list: An employee repeatedly makes the same mistake despite guidance.
The employee lacks necessary technical competence.
A task involves safety or client consent.
Training responsibilities are interfering with normal operations.
A new employee is being mocked or excluded.
Instructions from different colleagues conflict.
An employee refuses reasonable training.
An employee is being assigned duties beyond her training or authority.

sections.title: 21. Practical case studies
paragraphs: Use the four case studies below in discussion. Identify the unhelpful behaviour, the effect on learning, and the professional response.

sections.title: Case study A: The embarrassed new therapist
paragraphs: A new therapist asks an experienced colleague to explain a room-preparation procedure.
The colleague responds loudly: "How can you still not know this?"
The new therapist becomes embarrassed and stops asking questions.
Expected lesson: Employees should correct and guide others without humiliation.
list: What did the experienced therapist do wrong?
How might the response affect the new employee's confidence?
What could happen if the new therapist begins guessing?
How should the colleague have responded?
What should the supervisor do if the behaviour continues?

sections.title: Case study B: The experienced employee who withholds knowledge
paragraphs: An experienced receptionist knows the correct appointment-confirmation procedure.
A new receptionist asks for guidance.
The experienced employee refuses because she wants to remain the most knowledgeable person at reception.
Expected lesson: Sharing approved knowledge strengthens the entire team.
list: Why is withholding essential work knowledge harmful?
How might it affect clients?
What attitude should the experienced employee demonstrate?
How can management encourage knowledge-sharing?
What is the difference between healthy professional ambition and unhealthy competition?

sections.title: Case study C: The employee who depends on others
paragraphs: A new therapist has received training in a routine task.
However, she repeatedly asks colleagues to complete it for her instead of practising.
Other employees begin feeling frustrated.
Expected lesson: Support should encourage learning and accountability rather than dependence.
list: What responsibility belongs to the new therapist?
How can colleagues help without taking over?
What feedback should be provided?
When should the supervisor become involved?
How can the employee develop independence?

sections.title: Case study D: The excluded new colleague
paragraphs: A new employee joins Zura Spa.
Several existing employees have a close friendship group.
They regularly discuss work updates privately and do not include the new employee.
She misses an important procedural change.
Expected lesson: A professional team includes all employees who need relevant information.
list: What is the difference between friendship and exclusion?
Why should operational information be shared appropriately?
How might exclusion affect team performance?
What should the existing employees do differently?
How can supervisors ensure everyone receives important updates?

sections.title: 22. Practical group activity: Supportive or discouraging?
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees recognise the difference between constructive mentoring and discouraging workplace behaviour.
Read each situation and identify the best professional response before revealing the answer.

Role-play: Divide participants into pairs. One participant should act as a new employee who is struggling with a routine procedure. The other should act as an experienced colleague providing guidance. The experienced colleague should use the GUIDE method to explain the procedure, encourage questions and provide constructive feedback. Exchange roles afterward.
Expected outcome: Employees practise patient communication, mentoring and respectful correction.

items.label: 1. A new therapist asks the same reasonable question for the second time.
items.body: Explain patiently again. Identify the confusing step, use the checklist and practise together. Patience is not ignoring repeated mistakes forever — escalate ongoing training needs if they continue.

items.label: 2. A new receptionist makes an error while learning the appointment system.
items.body: Correct constructively. Name the specific gap, show the correct procedure and confirm understanding. Do not attack the person.

items.label: 3. An experienced employee believes a new colleague is learning faster than she did.
items.body: Share approved knowledge. Another person's competence does not reduce yours. Unhealthy competition weakens the team.

items.label: 4. A new employee asks for help while you are preparing for an imminent client appointment.
items.body: Protect your assigned duty first. Finish the appointment preparation, then help, or refer her to the supervisor if she needs assistance sooner.

items.label: 5. A new therapist is asked to perform a procedure for which she has not demonstrated competence.
items.body: Do not allow independent work. Arrange appropriate training or supervision. Client safety and service standards come first.

items.label: 6. A group of employees excludes a new colleague from important operational updates.
items.body: Share operational information through approved channels and include everyone who needs it. Friendships must not isolate new staff from work updates.

sections.title: 23. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 6 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the main purpose of supporting new employees? To complete all their work permanently / To help them develop competence, confidence and accountability / To make them dependent on experienced staff

A new employee asks a reasonable question about a procedure. What should an experienced colleague do? Explain the procedure respectfully and confirm understanding / Mock the employee for not knowing / Tell the employee to guess

What should happen when a new employee has not demonstrated competence in a safety-sensitive procedure? Allow independent work to build confidence / Ask another new employee to supervise / Arrange appropriate training or supervision before independent performance

Which behaviour demonstrates healthy knowledge-sharing? Withholding information to remain indispensable / Sharing approved procedures and helping colleagues learn / Excluding new employees from operational updates
What does the GUIDE method stand for? Greet, Understand, Instruct, Develop and Encourage / Guess, Undermine, Ignore, Discourage and Exclude / Give orders, Use criticism, Insult, Demand and Embarrass

sections.title: 24. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what supporting new and less-experienced staff means.
Describe the difference between being new and being inexperienced.
Identify five benefits of supporting new employees at Zura Spa.
Explain why experienced employees should avoid mocking colleagues who ask questions.
Describe how an experienced therapist can help a new therapist learn room-preparation procedures.
Explain the difference between helping someone learn and doing their work for them.
Describe how withholding knowledge can affect teamwork.
Explain why new employees should be included in relevant workplace communication.
Identify five responsibilities of a new employee during training.
Describe the GUIDE method in your own words.
Explain when a supervisor should arrange additional training or intervene in a mentoring situation.
Identify three practical ways you can contribute to a more supportive learning environment at Zura Spa.

sections.title: 25. Seven-day staff support challenge
table: Welcome or encourage a colleague who is still learning
Explain one approved procedure clearly to someone who needs guidance
Practise responding patiently to a reasonable question
Give constructive feedback without embarrassing the recipient
Share relevant workplace knowledge through the appropriate channel
Encourage a colleague to practise a task independently with appropriate support
Reflect on how your behaviour contributes to a supportive team culture

sections.title: 26. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Supporting new and less-experienced staff is an important responsibility in a healthy workplace.
At Zura Spa, employees should understand that nobody becomes experienced without learning.
New colleagues need clear instructions, patient guidance, constructive feedback and opportunities to practise.
Experienced employees should avoid mockery, unhealthy competition, deliberate exclusion and withholding important knowledge.
However, support must also encourage accountability.
New employees should listen, ask questions, practise, accept corrections and take responsibility for their improvement.
The goal is not to create dependence but to develop capable, confident and professional employees who can contribute meaningfully to the team.
Next topic: Cooperating During Busy or Stressful Periods.

remember: At some point, every experienced employee was a beginner. Someone explained a procedure, answered a question, offered guidance or provided an opportunity to learn. When a new colleague joins Zura Spa, do not see her inexperience as a reason to look down on her. See it as an opportunity to strengthen the team. Teach what you know, correct respectfully, encourage improvement and make room for others to grow. Your knowledge becomes more valuable when it helps others become competent. A strong team is not one where only a few people know how to do things well. It is one where employees continually help one another develop the skills, confidence and responsibility needed to deliver excellent service.
